title: Study Abroad Report: Medical University of Gdansk
paragraphs: Through the Nagoya University exchange program, I studied abroad at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland together with Mr. 小林. It was my first time overseas, so I felt half expectation and half anxiety, but I finished the clerkship safely and feel a sense of accomplishment and satisfaction and gratitude toward the many people. In the three months of study abroad, the content was two weeks of medical science, one week of psychiatry, two weeks of neurology, two weeks of hematology, three weeks of surgery, one week of vascular surgery and one week of clinical allergology.

On the university grounds there was an old student dormitory, and there the two of us began living in the same room. We first made greeting rounds of the dormitory, and I remember being very grateful that a Spanish exchange student we met there took a lot of care of us.

The first clinical subject I took, psychiatry, was held at a single-specialty hospital 5 km from the dormitory, something like Shiroyama Hospital in Nagoya. The basic clerkship style was a lecture of one to two hours, followed by medical interviews by group with a doctor's English interpretation. The first patient had schizophrenia, and because I was not yet used to English (especially Polish English, which reads R directly as "ru") and above all because of the patient's difficult medical history, I could not make progress in understanding and was helped by everyone in my group. Probably because of the national character, there seem to be many patients with alcohol dependence here, and I also examined those patients and patients such as those with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Next was neurology. I learned a great deal about neurodegenerative diseases such as Huntington's disease, corticobasal degeneration and cerebellar atrophy, demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and childhood epilepsy. In particular, I was given special private lessons by a doctor on the neurological examination, which was fulfilling. There were also patients who could speak English, and in the three weeks up to then I had finally become able to conduct simple interviews with such patients. I think it was the week from which I gained the most in these three months.

Another thing that left an impression was surgery. There is not as much of a concept of clean and unclean as in Japan, the hand gel after hand washing was a push-down type, the paper was no different from what is in the toilet, and it was along the lines of "put on gloves and it's fine." There were resection of an echinococcal cyst of the liver and removal of a giant spleen, all diseases I had hardly seen in Japan, so it was fresh. At the end of the week there was also a presentation contest, and I remember with fondness studying diverticulitis in the library with a fourth-year Swedish student in the English Division and presenting nervously. There was also a group presenting on sex reassignment surgery, which had a heated argument with a Polish doctor who, in a former socialist country, is somewhat conservative, and it was shocking.

We two also received instruction in medical science from Professor Wozniak of biochemistry. The topics were neuroprotection and improvement of memory. We were allowed to present this at the joint symposium with Italy and Japan held at the end of May. On that occasion Dr. 若林, who had formerly been a professor of biochemistry here, Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 近藤 and Dr. Gerry, who was studying here from China, came from Japan, and at dinner they told us valuable stories.

For extracurricular activities, I played futsal twice a week with the surgery professors and also took part in a full marathon. In the countryside English did not get through and it was sometimes hard, but basically there were many people who were fluent, and since everything from registration to procedures could be done in English, it was training in everyday English and let me feel the local atmosphere firsthand.

There was also quite a lot of interaction with students. Students from various countries around the world, centered on Europe, gather in the six-year English Division and the exchange program Erasmus, and I feel that by communicating with them I was taught about various differences in values. Overall they placed more importance on work-life balance than Japanese students and were oriented toward medicine as a business. What I noticed from talking with them is that Europeans and South Americans alike are incomparably better at English. They said it is because the word order is the same, or because the origin is the same Latin, but I felt that even we Japanese, who are poor at acquiring English, must shift to more practical conversational education and build up ability. I will keep learning.

I was also able to become friends with the Polish students living on the same floor, and playing in the grove in front of the dormitory and in their rooms are good memories. Perhaps because of the relatively low prices in the country, many students seem to go abroad, but I hope to meet them again somewhere.

It was three months in which one event came after another, and there was much stress from differences in living environment and language, and there were even situations in which I felt psychological pain. But I think I was able to overcome them by cooperating with Mr. 小林. Being able to deepen my friendship with a classmate in this way is one of the real pleasures of studying abroad, isn't it?

Finally, I would like to end by expressing my gratitude to Professor Wozniak and the doctors of the biochemistry department (Adam) who took care of us locally, to Dr. 粕谷 and the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, to the many students I got to know through study abroad (especially Yanusz, Piotr, Fillippo, Armando, Maciej, Szymon, Karolina, Duane, Dinal, Alvaro and Izabel), to the dormitory ladies, and to Mr. 小林.
